opening.headline: When each business unit has a different evaluation method making it impossible to compare results, we learn how to distinguish between what to standardize across all units and what to leave to individual business units.
body: Department A reports evaluations reviewed directly by humans, Department B uses automated metrics, and Department C relies on user satisfaction scores. Even if all reported values are between 0 and 1, the evaluation targets and input data differ across departments, making comparisons between them meaningless. Therefore, executives would find it difficult to determine which service has higher quality.

In this class, we first examine the five elements of evaluation design as described in OpenAI's evaluation documentation. Next, we read a common evaluation template that includes these elements and learn how to distinguish between common items, department-specific items, and minimum standards. Finally, we examine common items by using two example services: customer support and document summarization.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: You can explain what elements constitute the common evaluation criteria.
The evaluation areas of the service can be distinguished into common items and business unit-specific items.

screens.title: Each business division has a different evaluation method, making comparison impossible.
screens.lead: First, read how the evaluation reports from the three business units differ from each other.

visual.alt: Three evaluation reports issued by the three business divisions in different ways, and questions from the executive team.
labels: Division A: Review by a person

paragraphs: Let's assume the company has three business units, each operating AI services and evaluating their quality through reporting. Business Unit A uses results reviewed directly by humans, Business Unit B uses automatically calculated metrics, and Business Unit C relies on user satisfaction scores.

All three reports contain values between 0 and 1. However, even if the values appear similar, the specific measurements and the input data used to derive them differ. Therefore, executives cannot answer the question of which service has higher quality.

OpenAI's evaluation best practices document directly addresses this issue. It states that evaluations must be designed as structured processes, and relying on the impression that something "looks plausible" is considered an anti-pattern. The question posed in this course is: what should be reviewed collectively, and what should be delegated to the business units?

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Having the same numerical value does not mean they are comparable. To be comparable, the definition of the measurement subject and the data must be identical.

screens.outro: First, let's consider whether we can compare evaluation results within our organization currently.

screens.title: Can we compare the evaluation results among business units?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Can we compare the evaluation results among business units? If not, what is the primary reason?
items.answer: The reason comparisons fail is generally divided into four categories: different indicators, different data, different baseline values, or different evaluation timing. To determine which of these is the primary reason, we must identify what needs to be aligned consistently.

items.prompt: Do evaluation criteria match for services of the same type?
items.answer: It is common for items to be misaligned even among services of the same type. For example, if one customer service location adjusts its tone while another does not, the two cannot be compared. In such cases, it is necessary to first identify the common areas that align across both services.

items.prompt: Where and by whom are the evaluation results collected?
items.answer: If there is no place to collect results, there will be no way to align them using the same format. A common evaluation template also serves as a format for collecting results. To enable comparison, it must be determined who manages the template and where the results are collected.

screens.outro: First, let's examine what factors are involved in the design of an evaluation.

screens.title: Five Elements of Evaluation Design
screens.lead: When you select a card, it flips over to show an explanation. To move to the next card, select the right-arrow.

cards.back: Define the success criteria for evaluation. For example, for a summarization service, the model must achieve relevant and accurate performance comparable to the reference summary. Without a clear goal, one cannot select appropriate metrics.

Collects data to evaluate the goal. OpenAI documentation suggests considering synthetic data, data created by domain experts, purchased data, data curated by humans, operational data, and historical data. If evaluation data does not reflect patterns from operational traffic, biased design results.

We determine how to verify whether success criteria are satisfied. We list the metrics together with the benchmark values. For example, the summary example of a document specifies the metrics and benchmark values as "from 1,000 pending cases, achieving a ROUGE-L score of at least 0.40 and consistency of at least 80%."
Perform evaluation actually, compare results, and improve. To compare before-and-after changes, the evaluation must be repeated with the same input batch.

Set up continuous evaluation by assessing changes continuously, and during operations, expand evaluation groups to discover new non-deterministic cases. Evaluation is not a one-time event but an ongoing process.

screens.outro: These five elements form the core of a common evaluation template. Let's review a template example.

screens.title: Common Evaluation Template Example
screens.lead: The following is a hypothetical common evaluation template containing five elements. By selecting the indicated sections, you can see what each field represents. The benchmark values are examples for illustration purposes.

visual.alt: This is a one-page evaluation template format divided by item.
labels: All business units use the same template.

data.text:
Evaluation Objective: Follows system guidelines and provides responses that are factually accurate.  
Data Source: Operational data and expert-generated data  
Evaluation Scope: Compliance, functional accuracy  
Indicator and Benchmark: Classification accuracy 0.85 or higher (example value)  
Evaluation Cycle: Every time you change the model or prompt  
Responsible Party: Service Support Team  
Note: Automated scoring is adjusted to match human evaluation.

marks.span: Follows system guidelines and provides responses that are factually accurate.
marks.note: The first element of evaluation design is goal definition. Success criteria should be stated in a single sentence to clearly define what subsequent indicators and target values are measuring.
This pertains to data collection. The document recommends using data similar to operational traffic. Evaluating such data with data different from operations would result in biased design.

OpenAI's document identifies two evaluation areas for single-turn interactions. Instruction following assesses whether the model acts in accordance with the given instruction, while functional accuracy evaluates whether the output is both correct and sufficient. In tool-using scenarios, additional areas such as tool selection are included.

This cell contains both the indicator and the benchmark value. The document recommends evaluating the document in forms that allow for judgment, such as classification, paired comparison, or benchmark-based scoring, rather than open-ended generation.

marks.span: Every time you change the model or prompt
marks.note: This is a section related to continuous evaluation. Evaluation must be rerun after each change in order to immediately verify the impact of model replacement or prompt modifications.

marks.span: Automated scoring is adjusted to match human evaluation.
marks.note: The notice section contains principles for avoiding anti-patterns. The anti-patterns highlighted in the documentation are overly generic metrics, data unrelated to operations, evaluations based on subjective feelings, and the disregard of user feedback.

screens.outro: Having read the template, I will now separate what is common and what is unique within it.

screens.title: Common items, business unit unique items, minimum standards
screens.lead: Select each tab to see how these three concepts differ and how they interact with each other.

tabs.label: Common Items
tabs.body: All services fall within the same domain defined by a common standard. Areas such as compliance and functional accuracy are candidates, as they manifest regardless of service type. Common elements must have identical definitions and criteria formats to enable cross-business-unit comparison of results.

tabs.label: Business Unit Unique Item
tabs.body: Due to business characteristics, this area is separately defined by each business unit. For summary services, relevance and consistency are evaluated; for customer interaction services, intended classification accuracy and tone are assessed. Unique items are used to deeply evaluate service quality but are not used for comparison across different business units.

tabs.label: Minimum standard
tabs.body: This is the minimum threshold that all services must meet for common items. For example, it is illustrated by the summary example from the OpenAI documentation, which includes both metrics and benchmark values. If a minimum standard exists, services below this threshold can be filtered out at the corporate level.

tabs.label: Alignment
tabs.body: The common criteria establish a minimum baseline that enables corporate comparisons, while unique items add depth to on-site evaluations through additional areas. When both common and unique fields coexist within a single template, comparisons can be made above and deeper analysis can be conducted below.

screens.outro: Now, let's take two services as an example and actually select common items.

screens.title: Explanation: Common items between customer service and document summarization
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of identifying common items between the evaluation criteria of two services. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Two services are introduced.
steps.body: Customer service responds to retail inquiries by categorizing them and generating responses. Document summarization services summarize corporate reports. Although their tasks are different, both services use models.

steps.title: List each evaluation area.
steps.body: The evaluation criteria for customer service include intent classification accuracy, instruction adherence, and tone. The evaluation criteria for document summarization include relevance, consistency, and instruction adherence. First, the areas used by the business unit are listed verbatim.

steps.title: Find the overlapping area
steps.body: Find the overlapping area between the two lists. The common question is whether both services follow instructions and produce results that match reality. Intentional classification accuracy applies only to response generation, while relevance and consistency apply only to summarization.

steps.title: Common items are written in the same format.
steps.body: The overlapping areas are recorded in the template using the same definition and same reference format. If compliance is achieved, both services record in the same cell using the same method how judgments are made on inputs and what the reference values are.

steps.title: Leave the remaining area as a unique item
steps.body: The accuracy of tone and intent classification, as well as the relevance and consistency of summaries, are unique metrics for each business unit. These metrics are highly dependent on business characteristics and are therefore difficult to compare across units.

steps.title: result
steps.body: Compare two services using common items and examine them deeply through unique items. When asked which side better follows instructions, respond in the common field; when asked about customer service tone, respond in the unique field of the customer service department.

screens.outro: The number of common items to include is also an important judgment. We will examine this next.

screens.title: Explanation: The reason for maintaining the common standard at a minimum level
screens.lead: Compare the differences when transitioning between two states—when setting a common reference to be thick versus thin.

states.label: Thick common header
states.body:
This approach fixes all evaluation items uniformly across the organization. While comparison may appear simple, it fails to reflect service characteristics. For instance, critical aspects such as summary consistency or response tone do not align with standard forms and thus get omitted or awkwardly altered.

In practice, field staff only formally complete standard forms, conducting actual evaluations separately. As evaluation data and inspection targets increase, continuous evaluation becomes increasingly difficult. At a certain point, the cost of adhering to standard forms exceeds the benefits gained through comparison.

states.label: Thin common layer
states.body:
We maintain only the essential items required for comparison as common criteria, while delegating the rest as unique, business-unit-specific items. When the number of common criteria is small, the evaluation bundle and inspection costs are reduced, making it easier to sustain continuous evaluation upon each change.

Common criteria are reviewed regularly. Items that are no longer necessary are transferred back to the unique items, and any new areas found to be essential across all services are added to the common criteria. This ongoing refinement of standards is part of continuous evaluation.

In conclusion, we maintain the common criteria at a minimum and keep the scope of on-site evaluations open.

The question to decide between the two options is simple: if removing this item would make cross-business-unit comparison truly impossible, then it should remain in the common criteria; otherwise, it should be designated as a unique item.

screens.outro: Now I will summarize the composition of the common evaluation criteria once.

screens.title: Composition of Common Evaluation Criteria
screens.lead: We list the elements that constitute the common evaluation criteria in sequence.

paragraphs: **Evaluation Template**: Common evaluation criteria are expressed in evaluation templates. The target, data source, evaluation area, indicators and benchmark values, evaluation cycle, and responsible party are all listed in the same format. Templates must be identical so that results from different business units can be aligned side by side.

**Common Items and Unique Items**: Common items use the same definition and formatting standards, while business-unit-specific items reflect the unique characteristics of their operations. When both types are included within the same form, it enables comprehensive corporate comparisons and in-depth field evaluations.

**Minimum standard**: This is the lower bound that all services must exceed within the common items. The common standard is a minimum baseline for corporate comparisons and is therefore not made overly detailed.

callout.label: Core
callout.text: The common criteria are minimum requirements, while specific items are examined in depth by the business units.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded or graded.
checks.q: Arrange the five stages of evaluation design in the correct order.
checks.explain: Define success criteria, collect evaluation data, establish verification methods as metrics, then compare them in reverse, and continuously evaluate after each change.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. This follows the order of starting with objectives and progressing to continuous evaluation.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Take a closer look at the sequence again. You must first determine what was consumed in order to select the data and metrics.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded or graded.
checks.q: Listed evaluation criteria for customer interaction and document summarization. For interaction, the criteria were intent classification accuracy, instruction adherence, and tone. For summarization, the criteria were relevance, consistency, and instruction adherence. Which item is most appropriate to be included as a company-wide common criterion?
options: The tone of engagement — because it best demonstrates customer contact quality.
Consistency of summaries — because it can be easily expressed in numbers
Compliance — because the two services share an overlapping area defined by the same definition and standard format.
Intention classification accuracy — because it is a key performance indicator of customer service.
checks.explain: Common items involve defining and standardizing overlapping areas using the same definitions and criteria. Areas with strong business-specific characteristics, such as tone or consistency, are kept as department-specific items.

wrong.0: Tone applies only to customer service, thus it is a unique item of the Business Division.
wrong.1: This pertains only to the summary, thus it is a unique item. It does not become a common item merely because it is easily expressed numerically.
wrong.3: Classification accuracy is limited to customer service and cannot be used in general comparisons.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The area present in both services is a candidate for the common items.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think about it again. Look for the area that applies to both services.

glossary.def: All business units share the same definition for evaluation criteria and lower limits.
This is a document listing objectives, data, indicators, benchmark values, and periods in the same format.
Due to the nature of the work, this evaluation area is separately defined by the business unit.
This is the minimum threshold that all services must exceed in the common items.

misconceptions.myth: When evaluation criteria are unified across the entire company, quality improves.
misconceptions.fact: Excessive unification weakens field evaluations because it fails to reflect service characteristics. It is better to set common criteria at a minimum level necessary for comparison.

misconceptions.myth: Once the score is generated, the evaluation is complete.
misconceptions.fact: Do not look at indicators alone; they should be viewed together with human judgment. The document recommends adjusting automated scoring values to align with human evaluation.

misconceptions.myth: Different departments may have different evaluations, but numerical data alone can be compared.
misconceptions.fact: The definitions of the measurement target and input data must be identical for comparison. Even if both have the same values between 0 and 1, they cannot be compared if their definitions differ.

closing.lead: This summarizes the core content of the class.
points: The common standard is the minimum requirement.
Templates must be identical to compare business unit results.
Unique items are deeply examined by the business unit.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: In our organization's evaluation, what is the criterion that all business units must adhere to?
